title: Scalable Differential Privacy for Foundation Models: Pareto-Optimal Training, Auditing, and Certification
background:
Foundation models trained on web-scale corpora have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities, but mounting evidence shows they memorize and regurgitate training data, exposing personally identifiable information, copyrighted text, and proprietary code [1][3]. Differential privacy (DP), particularly DP-SGD, remains the gold standard for provable privacy, yet its naive application at the scale of modern transformers (10B-1T parameters) incurs prohibitive utility loss and 3-8x compute overhead due to per-example gradient clipping and noise injection [2]. Recent advances have narrowed this gap: ghost clipping and book-keeping techniques reduce memory overhead [2][4], group-wise clipping exploits transformer structure, and parameter-efficient DP fine-tuning (DP-LoRA, DP-Adapter) achieves competitive downstream accuracy at moderate epsilon budgets [4]. On the auditing side, membership inference and canary-based attacks now provide empirical lower bounds on realized privacy leakage, often revealing that analytical (epsilon, delta) bounds are loose by 1-2 orders of magnitude [5][6].

Despite this progress, fundamental gaps remain. First, no framework jointly optimizes the privacy-utility-compute Pareto frontier for pretraining-scale DP, where heterogeneous data sensitivity and long training horizons interact with privacy accountants in poorly understood ways [1][3]. Second, current auditing procedures are decoupled from training: they certify trained models post-hoc rather than producing tight, training-time certificates that adapt to data, architecture, and adversary capability [5][6]. Third, the unit of privacy (token, document, user) is rarely matched to deployment threat models, leading to either vacuous guarantees for user-level privacy or excessive noise. Fourth, emergent capabilities, RLHF, and multi-modal alignment introduce privacy channels (preference data, tool-use traces) that existing accountants do not cover [4]. Closing these gaps requires co-designed algorithms, accountants, and certification pipelines that scale to foundation-model regimes while remaining auditable by independent third parties.
challenges: Designing DP-SGD variants that scale to 100B+ parameter pretraining with sub-2x compute overhead, including efficient per-example gradient clipping under tensor/pipeline parallelism and noise calibration that exploits sparsity in attention and MoE layers.

Developing tight, composition-aware privacy accountants for heterogeneous training pipelines (pretraining + SFT + RLHF + tool-use), including user-level and group-level guarantees under data-dependent sampling and curriculum schedules.

Establishing training-time privacy auditing via adaptive canaries and f-DP lower bounds that produce certificates matching analytical guarantees within a small constant factor, rather than the current 10-100x looseness.

Characterizing and navigating the privacy-utility-fairness Pareto frontier across model scales, identifying when DP disproportionately harms underrepresented subpopulations and designing mitigations without violating the privacy contract.

Building reproducible third-party certification protocols and cryptographic attestations (e.g., TEE-backed training logs) so that downstream users and regulators can verify advertised (epsilon, delta) claims without access to raw training data.
